items.html:
Panama features short licence plates, most commonly white with a horizontal turquoise strip on the top. Rarely, the strip can have other colours.

Front plates are not required in Panama.

Panama was covered by a large white pickup truck that is usually entirely blurred. An antenna is occasionally visible.

NOTE: The Costa Rican truck is usually unblurred. The car used in Ecuador has neither an antenna nor a white metal railing.
Panama is a tropical country with a lot of hills. You will find a lot of palms and other tropical plants along with drier rolling hills and fields.
Most roads are paralleled by fences that are partly or fully made out of small trees. The rest of the fence posts are also almost always wooden.

Panamanian architecture often reflects Spanish colonial influences, featuring vibrant colours, and some ornate detailing. The most common type of building has painted concrete or sometimes brick walls with red metal sheets or tiles for a roof. Many windows have bars on them for security.

Panama features a diverse set of road lines, but the most common combination is solid outer white with an inner yellow line. However, those are not unique to Panama. Within Latin America, solid outer white lines with no middle line are almost unique to Panama.

Panama uses a wide variety of poles, but the most common type is a round concrete pole, with a varying amount of insulators. Poles can also be wooden or metallic. They often have plates attached to them. Blue, white, or red numbers are commonly painted on them as well.
Yellow taxis with a chequerboard patterned horizontal stripe are a common sight in Panama. The licence plate will be drawn on the side, containing the city name and a regional code.

Panama uses the Spanish word “ALTO” on stop signs.

NOTE: Mexico, Costa Rica and Guatemala also use “ALTO”, but the font is thinner.
Red octagonal signs with an oddly realistic eye are unique to Panama.
While Panama is quite well covered, there is barely any coverage on the north coast, or east of Panama City.

The first digit of phone numbers can be used to regionguess Panama.

The numbers with a smaller font indicate potentially useful regional two-digit codes.

NOTE: Only phone numbers with 7 digits are helpful, and any numbers starting with 5, 6, or 8 are useless as well.

The first digit of taxi and bus licence plates can be used to regionguess Panama.

NOTE: Cars travel, so they are not always reliable, especially outside of cities.
Green tropical landscapes with palm trees and very tall grass are common around Colón and Panama City.
Volcanic rocks that are either scattered on the ground, or built into rock walls, are common north of David.
The area around David is very flat, with lots of fairly open fields. Usually, mountains will be visible to the north and northeast.
The region around Aguadulce is relatively flat and features a lot of agricultural fields along with very brown or orange soil.

The eastern provinces often have tall vertical plates that can be yellow or white. They are commonly attached to poles by black zip ties.

NOTE: Be careful not to mix them up with these white vertical plates, often attached by metallic zip ties. They are slightly wider than the eastern plates and always have 6 digits.
Many poles in the western provinces will have horizontal plates attached to them. However, if one of these is accompanied by an eastern vertical plate, the eastern plate takes precedence.
Thin yellow plates, vertical or horizontal, with a visible black border are most common in the Colón Province.
Wind turbines can be seen south and north of Penonome.
The main covered road in the Ngäbe-Buglé province is very high-altitude and almost above the clouds. The surrounding mountains tend to be quite dry, and the altitude makes for many stunning views.
The road going to Changuinola features a lush and green hilly landscape. The weather is cloudy or overcast on the entire road.
Highway 9 going from Panama City north to Colón is a divided concrete highway. The road is visibly grainy and has a lot of tar lines. The landscape is lush and hilly.
Most of Road 407 features a freshly paved road, with visibly orange soil on the sides of the road. The southern portion is hilly, right before the road quality deteriorates.
Panama City can be recognised by the large number of white high-rise buildings.
Colón features a lot of warehouses and rundown multi-storey buildings.
The region around Changuinola is filled with banana plantations.
Sunset coverage can be found in southern Panama on a small road south of Tonosi.
A mountainous landscape with pine trees, volcanic rocks, dry grass, and gravel roads can be found northeast of Volcán.
Yellow pole socks can be found near the Panama Canal, around the town of Gatún.

steps.title: Maps and resources
steps.html:
GeoGuessr’s own official maps are not very good, for a variety of reasons. Plonk It recommends the following maps instead:

  • AI Generated Panama (map link) - 35k arbitrarily generated locations, balanced with streaking in mind. Not pinpointable.

In addition, here are some resources to help you practise Panama:

  • Plonk It Panama (map link) - This map contains locations for practising each meta in the Plonk It Panama guide from step 2 to 3.
  • Panama: Provinces Quiz on Seterra (quiz link) - Study the provinces of Panama using this quiz.
  • Panama: Taxi codes quiz on Seterra by Kommu (quiz link) - Study the taxi and bus codes of Panama using this quiz.

lm.name: Panama
lm.note:
The first digit of phone numbers can be used to regionguess Panama.

The numbers with a smaller font indicate potentially useful regional two-digit codes.

NOTE: Only phone numbers with 7 digits are helpful, and any numbers starting with 5, 6, or 8 are useless as well.

lm.name: 1 barely visible left dot - around David
lm.note: This very small dot to the left is common north and west of David.

lm.name: 1 bottom stain - east
lm.note: A small cluster of dirt on the car can be found on the eastern road.

lm.name: 1 dot right - Northwest
lm.note: This car with a small stain to the right is only found between Gualaca District and Changuinola.

lm.name: 1 or 2 left dots - central
lm.note: In a lot of central Panama, the Google car will have either one or two black dots visible on the front.

lm.name: Banana plantations - around Changuinola
lm.note: The region around Changuinola is filled with banana plantations.

lm.name: Bike lane - Pesé - Chitre
lm.note: Road 50 is the only one in Panama to have a bike lane, from Pesé to Chitre

lm.name: Cerro Trinidad - West of Capira
lm.note: Cerro Trinidad is a recognizable mountain with exposed rocky slopes west of Capira.

lm.name: Divided grainy Highway - Highway 9
lm.note: Highway 9 going from Panama City north to Colón is a divided concrete highway. The road is visibly grainy and has a lot of tar lines. The landscape is lush and hilly.

lm.name: Divided Highway + Barù volcano - Road 41
lm.note: Highway 41 is one of the 6 divided highways of the country. It is pretty easy to recognize because it is the one going to the Barù volcano, so it is sloping and the volcano is visible 90% of the time.

lm.name: Finca - Northwest
lm.note: Cities of Changuinola, Torres Bluff and Guabito name their suburbs the same way : “(Finca) Las XX” ,“XX” being the suburb number. They are the only cities where it is done that way.

lm.name: flat, brown or orange soil - around Aguadulce
lm.note: The region around Aguadulce is relatively flat and features a lot of agricultural fields along with very brown or orange soil.

lm.name: Flat, open fields - around David
lm.note: The area around David is very flat, with lots of fairly open fields. Usually, mountains will be visible to the north and northeast.

lm.name: Freshly Paved - Road 407
lm.note: Road 407 from Boca Chica to the junction with the panamerican highway has been concreted recently. Some parts of it are still dirt and under construction while some are concreted with dotted road lines.

lm.name: High altitude + dry mountains - Ngäbe-Buglé province
lm.note: The main covered road in the Ngäbe-Buglé province is very high-altitude and almost above the clouds. The surrounding mountains tend to be quite dry, and the altitude makes for many stunning views.

lm.name: Horizontal plate - western
lm.note: Many poles in the western provinces will have horizontal plates attached to them. However, if one of these is accompanied by an eastern vertical plate, the eastern plate takes precedence.

lm.name: Lowered Antenna - mostly Colon and Panama City
lm.note: The antenna can be seen folded down, most commonly in Colón and Panamá provinces, and occasionally in the city of David.

lm.name: Lush green + overcast -  road going to Changuinola
lm.note: The road going to Changuinola features a lush and green hilly landscape. The weather is cloudy or overcast on the entire road.

lm.name: Meseta de Chorcha - east of David
lm.note: On a small stretch of the panamerican highway east of David, a rocky formation, Meseta de Chorcha, can be seen. It is a very distinct elevation point and is unique in this region.

lm.name: MOP sticker - Central, rarely west
lm.note: MOP-sticker -The sticker is always black and small -Only in these 5 states, but for Coclé and Veraguas there by far mostly in the south of the state and in Chiriqui not that common -The highway in southern Veraguas almost has this sticker on every sign

lm.name: MOP sticker big - Max. east
lm.note: MOP-paint -This again reads ‘MOP’ with its logo and all. This time it has a lot of text above the logo -The difference, obviously, is that it's black paint (not a sticker) and it's very big -Only on the green part of the CA-1 in Darién but this time it's on most of the signs along the road

lm.name: Phone Code 2 - Capital & east
lm.note: Phone codes starting with 2 are found in Panama City and the east.

lm.name: Phone Code 4 - Colon Province
lm.note: Phone codes starting with 4 are found in Colon.

lm.name: Phone Code 7 - Bocas del Toro & Chiriquí
lm.note: Phone codes starting with 7 are found in the west.

lm.name: Phone Code 9 - central states
lm.note: Phone codes starting with 9 are found in Coclé, Herrera, Los Santos & Veraguas.

lm.name: Red dot on the right - Panamá Oeste & road 2
lm.note: This small red spot can mostly be found in Panamá Oeste and on the road 2 going from southern Los Santos province to the Verguas province. Note: Road 2 is the only divided road with this car.

lm.name: Sunset - South of Tonosi
lm.note: Sunset coverage can be found in southern Panama on a small road south of Tonosi. The more south you go, the lower the sun.

lm.name: Taxi Code 1 - Bocas del Toro
lm.note: Just like Colombian taxis, taxis in Panama are yellow and have the name of the city/province labeled on them. It is sometimes hard to read Panama Taxis plates, especially the name of the province/city.

lm.name: Taxi Code 3 - Colon
lm.note: Just like Colombian taxis, taxis in Panama are yellow and have the name of the city/province labeled on them. It is sometimes hard to read Panama Taxis plates, especially the name of the province/city.

lm.name: Taxi Code 4 - Chiriqui
lm.note: Just like Colombian taxis, taxis in Panama are yellow and have the name of the city/province labeled on them. It is sometimes hard to read Panama Taxis plates, especially the name of the province/city.

lm.name: Taxi Code 5 - Darien
lm.note: Just like Colombian taxis, taxis in Panama are yellow and have the name of the city/province labeled on them. It is sometimes hard to read Panama Taxis plates, especially the name of the province/city.

lm.name: Taxi Code 8 - Panama Province
lm.note: Just like Colombian taxis, taxis in Panama are yellow and have the name of the city/province labeled on them. It is sometimes hard to read Panama Taxis plates, especially the name of the province/city.

lm.name: Taxi Code 9 - Veraguas
lm.note: Just like Colombian taxis, taxis in Panama are yellow and have the name of the city/province labeled on them. It is sometimes hard to read Panama Taxis plates, especially the name of the province/city.

lm.name: Thin yellow plate - mostly Colón Province
lm.note: Thin yellow plates, vertical or horizontal, with a visible black border are most common in the Colón Province.

lm.name: Triangle dots - Southwest of Panama City
lm.note: This triangle of dots on the front right of the car is common southwest of the capital.

lm.name: Tropical landscape - around Colón and Panama City
lm.note: Green tropical landscapes with palm trees and very tall grass are common around Colón and Panama City.

lm.name: Vertical Plate - eastern
lm.note: The eastern provinces often have tall vertical plates that can be yellow or white. They are commonly attached to poles by black zip ties.

lm.name: Volcanic rock - North of David
lm.note: Volcanic rocks that are either scattered on the ground, or built into rock walls, are common north of David.

lm.name: Volcanic rock + dry + pines - Northeast of Volcán
lm.note: A mountainous landscape with pine trees, volcanic rocks, dry grass, and gravel roads can be found northeast of Volcán.

lm.name: Warehouses & rundown multi - Colon
lm.note: Colón features a lot of warehouses and rundown multi-storey buildings.

lm.name: White high rise buildings - Panama City
lm.note: Panama City can be recognised by the large number of white high-rise buildings.

lm.name: Wind turbines - around Penonome
lm.note: Northern: in the mountains, southern: in a flat area

lm.name: Yellow pole socks - around Gatún
lm.note: Yellow pole socks can be found near the Panama Canal, around the town of Gatún.

lm.name: Roadlines
lm.note:
• Panama features a diverse set of road lines, but the most common combination is solid outer white with an inner yellow line. However, those are not unique to Panama.
  • Within Latin America, solid outer white lines with no middle line are almost unique to Panama.

lm.name: horizontal marker
lm.note: East of Panama City and around Colon, utility pole marker are white or yellow and vertical.

lm.name: round concrete
lm.note:
Panama uses a wide variety of poles, but the most common type is a round concrete pole.

NOTE: Kenya has most of the time wooden poles with metallic support while Panama typically use wooden support.

lm.name: thin vertical marker
lm.note: Thin yellow plates, vertical or horizontal, with a visible black border are most common in the Colón Province.

lm.name: vertical marker
lm.note:
The eastern provinces often have tall vertical plates that can be yellow or white. They are commonly attached to poles by black zip ties.

NOTE: Be careful there are white vertical plates, often attached by metallic zip ties. They are slightly wider than the eastern plates and always have 6 digits.
